query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The relatively low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise because the simple solid‐solution state produces limited lattice distortion and weak solid solution hardening; as a result, grain-boundary-mediated deformation (such as intergranular sliding) predominates over dislocation accumulation, reducing the resistance to plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple, single-phase solid solution with a nanocrystalline grain structure.
generation.intervention: Varying the grain size through controlled thermal annealing to modify grain boundary density, while subjecting the material to standardized mechanical tests (e.g., nanoindentation and compression).
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing with controlled strain rates; specimens prepared in two states – as-cast (nanocrystalline) and annealed (with larger grains); composition maintained near equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries in the nanocrystalline structure and the uniform, low lattice distortion environment in the simple solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Due to the uniform elemental distribution, there is insufficient lattice distortion to significantly impede dislocation motion via solid-solution hardening. Consequently, the easy activation of grain-boundary sliding and related intergranular mechanisms limits the strengthening normally provided by dislocation interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, then maintaining a highly nanocrystalline microstructure should consistently yield lower hardness and strength due to predominant grain-boundary sliding. Conversely, annealing that increases the grain size (thereby reducing grain boundary area) should shift the deformation mode toward more dislocation-mediated plasticity and result in measurable increases in hardness and yield strength relative to the as-cast state.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (hardness, yield strength) measured in the as-cast, nanocrystalline equimolar CoCrFeNiTi state.
generation.boundary: Applicable to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys in a simple solid-solution state with nanocrystalline grain sizes (typically <50 nm), under room-temperature deformation conditions and moderate strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effect of grain size changes on mechanical properties is uncertain without direct experimental measurement. Moreover, potential influences from minor elemental segregation or impurities are not fully ruled out.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi specimens: one set retained in the as-cast nanocrystalline state and a second set subjected to annealing to promote grain growth. Conduct nanoindentation and uniaxial compression tests while performing in situ microscopic observation (e.g., SEM) to evaluate the dominant deformation mechanism (grain-boundary sliding versus dislocation motion).
measurements: Yield strength and stress–strain behavior (from compression tests)
Microstructural analysis of deformed regions (fracture surface and in situ SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples (with reduced grain boundary density) do not exhibit a significant increase in hardness and yield strength compared to the as-cast specimens, or if both conditions show evidence of predominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity rather than grain-boundary sliding, then the mechanism posited by the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement

Question: How can the compressive strength of the NbMoCrTiAl refractory high-entropy alloy be improved for high-temperature structural applications while maintaining oxidation resistance?. System: NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy matrix with in-situ formed TiC and Al2O3 reinforcement particles. Processing: High energy planetary ball milling for 39 h at 300 rpm with stearic acid as process control agent, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1700 °C under 30 MPa axial pressure for 30 min.
